transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Election day may be over, but votes are still being counted and results are still coming
in.
It comes after a blockbuster night for Democrats who flipped key seats in the U.S. Senate and
House.
NPR's Elena Moore has this update on where things stand.
So far, Democrats have flipped 29 seats in the House, according to race calls by the
Associated Press, and more are likely, with Democratic candidates up in dozens of additional
races that have yet to be called.
On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped a whopping seven seats, with wins in Kansas,
Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, and Ohio.
A few tight races remain too early to call, notably Alaska and Mississippi.
Alaska was expected to be close.
It was seen as a toss-up race heading into Election Day.
But historically, Ruby Red, Mississippi, was not expected to be this close.
Ballots are still being counted, but the candidates are essentially tied.
Elena Moore, NPR News.
House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress,
NPR's Barbara Sprunt reports.
The Louisiana Republican served two terms as Speaker.
Elected after his predecessor, Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023.
His departure will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority.
Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on November 10th.
Johnson endured a balancing act trying to keep his conference united.
With a razor-thin majority, even one Republican defectionist Congress meant GOP leadership
priorities were at risk.
Barbara Sprunt, NPR News, Washington.
Iranian officials celebrated the U.S. midterm election results.
Concerns about the Iran war and its impact on fuel prices helped the Democrats win control
of Congress.
On social media, Iran's chief negotiator praised Americans for saying "no" to war.
The region remains on edge over possible renewed U.S. military operations against Iran.
Talks continue, with Israel pressing for more strikes and other allies urging restraint.
Recent strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz have raised questions about the
Trump administration's next steps.
A former federal prosecutor has been picked to lead New York State's investigation into
the Cornell sexual assault case, and PR's Alyssa Nadwirny reports.
The New York Attorney General has appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell graduate who helped
prosecute musician Sean Diddy Combs, to be the outside counsel directing the investigation.
Kelly works for a private law firm and used to head the Criminal Civil Rights Division
in the U.S. Attorney General's office in Manhattan.
She and her team of lawyers from the AG's office and her firm will look for evidence
from the 2024 assault, including previous investigative records, and they'll also be
tasked with gathering new details and conducting fresh witness interviews.
Alyssa Nadwirny, NPR News.
U.S. stocks soared after Republicans lost sole control of Washington in the midterm
elections.
Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who
wins.
The Dow surged more than 1,500 points, or 3 percent.
It's NPR.
Launch authorities say a cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to
dangerous levels, but was stopped before causing damage.
The attack happened Monday at three cold storage sites for plasma.
Monitoring systems detected the problem, allowing staff to act quickly.
The incident follows similar attacks on supermarkets in Europe, where fridges and freezers were
remotely taken over spoiling food.
Nebraska and Arizona voters approved ballot measures restricting participation by trans
girls and women in school sports yesterday.
NPR's Becky Sullivan reports results are still too close to call in two other states.
Arizona voters approved a law to restrict teams to the sex of athletes as assigned at
birth, and banned trans students from restrooms and locker rooms of their expressed identity.
And Nebraska voters enshrined an existing trans athlete ban into the state's constitution.
Meanwhile, measures in two blue states, Colorado and Washington, are still too close to call.
The Colorado proposal would require student athletes from kindergarten through college
to participate on teams that match their sex assigned at birth, boys and girls alike.
Washington's measure would apply only to K-12 girls sports, but it would also require
all female athletes to provide medical documentation that confirms their biological sex.
Votes are still being counted.
The yes vote was ahead in both states.
Becky Sullivan, NPR News.
One of NASA's premier space telescopes has plunged to Earth, ending its 22-year investigation
of the universe's biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory's demise came after the failure of a long-shot rescue mission involving
a three-armed robotic craft that came crashing down in September.
One could say it was the end of an era for the Swift Observatory.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Democrats flip 29 House seats and seven Senate seats; Alaska and Mississippi races remain too close to call
House Speaker Mike Johnson will not stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress
Iranian officials celebrate U.S. midterm results, crediting opposition to war for Democratic gains
Former federal prosecutor Jacqueline Kelly appointed to lead New York investigation into Cornell sexual assault case
U.S. stocks surge, with the Dow gaining more than 1,500 points after Republicans lose sole control of Congress
Cyberattack on three plasma blood bank cold storage sites attempting to raise temperatures is stopped
Nebraska and Arizona voters approve restrictions on trans athletes; Colorado and Washington measures too close to call
NASA's Swift Observatory plunges to Earth, ending its 22-year mission studying cosmic explosions
